questions.stemHtml: A 24-year-old woman with a history of leukemia presents one month after a bone marrow transplant with a widespread scaling rash. She received a partially mismatched donor marrow. A skin biopsy is performed, and the histopathological findings show the presence of apoptotic cells. Which of the following biochemical reactions most likely explains these findings?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Activation of caspases

 

  • The histopathological findings in the skin biopsy, which show apoptotic cells, are indicative of graft-versus-host disease (GVHD).
  • In GVHD, donor immune cells attack the recipient's tissues, leading to apoptosis.
  • Apoptosis is mediated by a cascade of biochemical events involving the activation of caspases.
  • Caspases are proteolytic enzymes that play a crucial role in the execution phase of cell apoptosis, leading to the orderly and programmed dismantling of cellular components.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Reduction of ATP synthesis: This is typically associated with cellular necrosis rather than apoptosis. Necrosis results from severe ATP depletion and is characterized by cell swelling and rupture, not the orderly process seen in apoptosis.

 

Option B. Increase in glycolysis: While an increase in glycolysis can occur in various conditions, it is not specifically related to the apoptotic changes seen in this biopsy.

 

Option C. Activation of lipases: Lipase activation can occur in the context of cell injury leading to necrosis, particularly in the pancreas, but it is not directly related to the apoptotic process observed here.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • The presence of apoptotic cells in a skin biopsy from a patient with a scaling rash after a bone marrow transplant is indicative of graft-versus-host disease, driven by the activation of caspases, leading to programmed cell death (apoptosis).

questions.stem: A 6-year-old child is brought to the clinic with a history of recurrent bacterial infections, including pneumonia and otitis media. Laboratory analysis of leukocytes reveals a deficiency in myeloperoxidase. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this child's increased susceptibility to infections?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Failure to produce hydroxy-halide radicals (HOCl⁻)

 

  • Myeloperoxidase (MPO) is an enzyme present in neutrophils that converts hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) and chloride ions (Cl⁻) into hypochlorous acid (HOCl) during the respiratory burst.
  • Hypochlorous acid is a potent antimicrobial agent that plays a critical role in killing bacteria and other pathogens.
  • A deficiency in MPO leads to the failure to produce HOCl, significantly impairing the neutrophils' ability to destroy ingested microbes, thus resulting in increased susceptibility to infections.

 

Other Options

 

Option A. Defective neutrophil degranulation: While defective degranulation affects the release of antimicrobial substances from neutrophil granules, the specific deficiency in MPO is more directly related to the failure to produce HOCl.

 

Option B. Failure to produce hydrogen peroxide: Hydrogen peroxide is produced by the NADPH oxidase complex. A failure to produce hydrogen peroxide is associated with chronic granulomatous disease (CGD), not MPO deficiency.

 

Option D. Decreased oxygen consumption after phagocytosis: This is indicative of chronic granulomatous disease, where the defect is in the NADPH oxidase complex leading to an inability to produce reactive oxygen species, which is distinct from MPO deficiency.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Myeloperoxidase deficiency leads to the failure to produce hypochlorous acid (HOCl), a crucial antimicrobial agent, resulting in increased susceptibility to infections.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man presents with marked abdominal pain, diffuse abdominal tenderness, and decreased bowel sounds. Laboratory studies show a serum creatinine level of 4.4 mg/dL and a blood urea nitrogen level of 42 mg/dL. Renal biopsy reveals focal fibrinoid necrosis of small arteries and arterioles with intravascular microthrombi and scattered neutrophils. Which of the following laboratory findings would most likely be present in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Decreased complement C3

 

  • The clinical and histological findings suggest systemic vasculitis, such as polyarteritis nodosa (PAN), which is often associated with decreased levels of complement due to consumption during the inflammatory process.
  • The presence of focal fibrinoid necrosis and intravascular microthrombi with scattered neutrophils is typical for vasculitis.
  • Decreased complement C3 levels indicate active consumption in immune complex-mediated damage.

 

Other Options

 

Option B. Neutropenia: Not associated with vasculitis characterized by fibrinoid necrosis.

 

Option C. Increased IgE: Seen in allergic conditions and parasitic infections, not vasculitis.

 

Option D. CD4+ lymphocytosis: Associated with chronic infections like HIV, not acute vasculitis.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Decreased complement C3 levels are indicative of immune complex-mediated vasculitis, such as polyarteritis nodosa, characterized by focal fibrinoid necrosis and microthrombi in small arteries and arterioles.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old man presents with a one-year history of abdominal pain. An abdominal CT scan shows a 10-cm mass in the pancreas. Biopsy reveals adenocarcinoma with inactivation of SMAD4. Which regulatory pathway is most likely altered?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) TGF-β

 

  • The inactivation of SMAD4 in pancreatic adenocarcinoma suggests an alteration in the TGF-β (transforming growth factor-beta) pathway.
  • SMAD4 is a key signal transducer in the TGF-β signaling pathway, which is involved in the regulation of cell growth, differentiation, and apoptosis.
  • Loss of SMAD4 function impairs TGF-β signaling, resulting in uncontrolled cell proliferation and tumor growth.

 

Other Options

 

Option A. BCL2: This gene is involved in regulating apoptosis by preventing cell death. It is not directly related to SMAD4 or the TGF-β pathway.

 

Option B. β-catenin: This protein is part of the Wnt signaling pathway and is involved in cell adhesion and transcription regulation. It is not associated with SMAD4 in the context described.

 

Option C. MYC: This oncogene regulates cell proliferation, growth, and apoptosis. While MYC can be altered in various cancers, it is not directly linked to the SMAD4 and TGF-β pathway.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Inactivation of SMAD4 in pancreatic adenocarcinoma disrupts the TGF-β signaling pathway, leading to diminished transcriptional activation of cyclin-dependent kinases and contributing to tumor growth.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old child presents with a 10-day history of abdominal pain, dark urine, and purpuric skin lesions. Urinalysis shows hematuria and proteinuria. Serologic tests are negative for P-ANCAs and C-ANCAs. Skin biopsy reveals necrotizing vasculitis of small dermal vessels, and renal biopsy shows IgA-rich immune complex deposition. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Henoch-Schönlein purpura

 

  • Henoch-Schönlein purpura (HSP) is a small vessel vasculitis primarily affecting children.
  • It is characterized by the deposition of IgA immune complexes in small vessels.
  • The clinical presentation typically includes a triad of palpable purpura, abdominal pain, and renal involvement, such as hematuria and proteinuria.
  • The biopsy findings of necrotizing vasculitis in the dermis and IgA deposition in the glomeruli are consistent with HSP.

 

Other Options

 

Option B. Takayasu arteritis: This vasculitis affects large arteries, particularly the aorta and its branches, and is not associated with IgA deposition or the described clinical features in children.

 

Option C. Wegener granulomatosis (Granulomatosis with polyangiitis): This condition involves granulomatous inflammation affecting the respiratory tract and kidneys and is associated with ANCA positivity, not IgA deposition.

 

Option D. Giant cell arteritis: This vasculitis affects large and medium-sized arteries and primarily occurs in older adults, not in children.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Henoch-Schönlein purpura (HSP) is a small vessel vasculitis characterized by IgA deposition, presenting with palpable purpura, abdominal pain, and renal involvement, making it the most likely diagnosis in this scenario.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man presents with increasing dyspnea for the past week. Physical examination reveals a temperature of 37.3°C, pulse 85/min, and blood pressure 150/95 mm Hg. There is dullness to percussion over the lung bases. Laboratory findings include serum creatinine 3.1 mg/dL, urea nitrogen 29 mg/dL, troponin I 0.1 ng/mL, hemoglobin 11.7 g/dL, and positive ANA and anti-double-stranded DNA antibody test results. Which of the following cardiac lesions is most likely to be present in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Libman-Sacks endocarditis

 

  • Libman-Sacks endocarditis is a form of nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis commonly associated with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).
  • The patient's positive ANA and anti-double-stranded DNA antibody test results indicate an autoimmune process consistent with SLE.
  • The presence of bilateral pleural effusions, elevated serum creatinine, and urea nitrogen levels further supports the diagnosis of SLE, which can involve multiple organs, including the kidneys and serosal surfaces. Libman-Sacks endocarditis involves vegetations on the heart valves, which are typically sterile but can cause valvular dysfunction.

 

Other Options

 

Option A. Calcific aortic stenosis: This condition is characterized by calcification and narrowing of the aortic valve, leading to symptoms like angina, syncope, and heart failure, but it is not associated with positive ANA and anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies.

 

Option B. Constrictive pericarditis: This results from the thickening and calcification of the pericardium, restricting heart movement, but it is not typically associated with SLE or the serological findings presented.

 

Option C. Ischemic cardiomyopathy: This condition results from chronic ischemic heart disease leading to heart failure but is not associated with positive autoimmune markers or the described clinical scenario.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Libman-Sacks endocarditis is associated with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and presents with nonbacterial vegetations on heart valves.
  • Positive ANA and anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies are indicative of SLE, making Libman-Sacks endocarditis the most likely cardiac lesion in this patient.

questions.stem: A 53-year-old man presents with fatigue, weight loss, and splenomegaly. Laboratory tests reveal an elevated white blood cell count. Cytogenetic analysis shows the BCR-ABL fusion gene resulting from the t(9;22)(q34;q11) translocation. Which condition is most likely associated with this genetic finding?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Chronic myelogenous leukemia

 

  • The BCR-ABL fusion gene, resulting from the t(9;22)(q34;q11) translocation, is known as the Philadelphia chromosome and is characteristic of chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML).
  • This fusion gene encodes an abnormal tyrosine kinase that leads to uncontrolled cell proliferation, a hallmark of CML.

 

Other Options

 

Option A. Acute promyelocytic leukemia: This condition is associated with the t(15;17) translocation involving the PML-RARA gene, not BCR-ABL.

 

Option B. Follicular lymphoma: This is typically associated with the t(14;18) translocation involving the BCL2 gene, not BCR-ABL.

 

Option D. Hodgkin lymphoma, lymphocyte depletion type: This is not associated with the BCR-ABL fusion gene or the t(9;22) translocation.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • The BCR-ABL fusion gene from the t(9;22) translocation is specifically associated with chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML), leading to uncontrolled proliferation of leukemic cells.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old boy presents with dark urine, a history of bacterial infections, and venous thromboses, including portal vein thrombosis. Examination shows a swollen, tender right leg. Labs: Hb 9.8 g/dL, Hct 29.9%, MCV 92 µm³, platelets 150,000/mm³, WBC 3800/mm³. He has reticulocytosis and very low serum haptoglobin. Which gene mutation is likely responsible?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Phosphatidylinositol glycan A (PIGA)

 

  • The clinical presentation suggests paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH), which is caused by a mutation in the PIGA gene.
  • This gene is essential for the synthesis of glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchors, which attach protective proteins to the cell surface.
  • The absence of these proteins on red blood cells leads to increased susceptibility to complement-mediated lysis, resulting in hemolysis, dark urine (due to hemoglobinuria), low haptoglobin levels, and increased risk of thrombosis.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase: Deficiency in this enzyme causes G6PD deficiency, leading to episodic hemolysis triggered by oxidative stress, but it does not explain the chronic symptoms and thrombosis seen in this patient.

 

Option B. Spectrin: Mutations in spectrin are associated with hereditary spherocytosis, which causes hemolytic anemia but not the specific combination of symptoms, including thrombosis, seen in PNH.

 

Option C. β-Globin chain: Mutations in the β-globin chain are responsible for conditions like sickle cell disease and β-thalassemia, which do not align with this patient's presentation.

 

Educational objective:

 

  • Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH) is associated with mutations in the PIGA gene, leading to defective GPI anchors and resulting in hemolysis, hemoglobinuria, and an increased risk of thrombosis.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old man has experienced increasing respiratory difficulty for the past 18 months, preventing him from passing his yearly physical examination as an airline pilot. Physical examination is unremarkable. Pulmonary function tests show normal FEV1 but diminished FVC. A chest radiograph reveals diffuse interstitial disease without masses or hilar adenopathy. ANA and anti-DNA topoisomerase I antibody tests are negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis

 

  • Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is characterized by progressive interstitial lung disease leading to restrictive lung disease, evidenced by normal FEV₁ and reduced FVC.
  • Chest radiographs typically show diffuse interstitial changes.
  • The absence of autoimmune markers such as ANA and anti-DNA topoisomerase I supports the diagnosis of IPF over other conditions.

 

Other Options

 

Option A. Goodpasture syndrome: Typically involves hemoptysis and renal involvement, with anti-GBM antibodies.

 

Option B. Scleroderma: Often associated with positive ANA or anti-DNA topoisomerase I antibodies.

 

Option C. Diffuse alveolar damage: More typical of acute conditions like ARDS, not a chronic, progressive disease.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis is a chronic, progressive interstitial lung disease characterized by restrictive lung patterns on PFTs and diffuse interstitial changes on radiographs, without autoimmune marker positivity.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man has a 6-kg weight loss and nausea for the past 7 months without vomiting or diarrhea. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy reveals a 6-cm area of irregular, pale fundic mucosa and loss of rugal folds. Helicobacter pylori organisms are identified in mucus overlying adjacent mucosa. After antibiotic therapy for H. pylori, a repeat biopsy shows resolution of the infiltrate. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue tumor

 

  • The resolution of the lymphoid infiltrate after antibiotic therapy for Helicobacter pylori indicates a mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) tumor.
  • MALT lymphomas are often associated with chronic H. pylori infection, and eradication of the infection can lead to tumor regression.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Chronic gastritis: While chronic gastritis can be associated with H. pylori, it does not explain the lymphoid infiltrate and resolution after treatment.

 

Option B. Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma: This type of lymphoma would not typically resolve with antibiotic therapy for H. pylori.

 

Option C. Autoimmune gastritis: This condition is characterized by autoantibodies against parietal cells, not by H. pylori infection or lymphoid infiltrates.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) tumors are associated with H. pylori infection and can regress after eradication of the bacteria.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man, who was recently found to have renal vein thrombosis, is under medical review. His medical history includes significant weight gain, generalized edema, and hypertension. His urine analysis reveals significant proteinuria and the presence of numerous normal-looking red blood cells without any casts. Tests also show positive anti-PLA2R antibodies. Based on these findings, what would you expect to see on his renal biopsy?

options.label: A
options.text: Diffuse thickening of the GBM with a spike and dome pattern

questions.answerText: Diffuse thickening of the GBM with a spike and dome pattern
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Diffuse thickening of the GBM with spike and dome pattern

 

  • The presence of anti-PLA2R antibodies is highly suggestive of primary membranous nephropathy. This autoimmune disorder is characterized histologically by diffuse thickening of the glomerular basement membrane (GBM) due to subepithelial immune deposits.
  • These deposits can lead to the formation of a "spike and dome" pattern on silver staining of the renal biopsy, which is a classic finding in this condition.
  • The combination of gross proteinuria and the specific antibody presence further supports this diagnosis.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Tram-track appearance of the GBM: This finding is typical of membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN), which is associated with immune complex deposition and complement activation within the GBM and mesangium. It is not indicative of membranous nephropathy.

 

Option C. Mesangial deposition of IgA: The presence of IgA in the mesangium is characteristic of IgA nephropathy (Berger’s disease), which does not correlate with the presence of anti-PLA2R antibodies and is differentiated by its immunofluorescence staining patterns.

 

Option D. Large and hypercellular glomeruli: This description fits with proliferative forms of glomerulonephritis, such as lupus nephritis or acute post-infectious glomerulonephritis, rather than membranous nephropathy.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In a patient presenting with symptoms of nephrotic syndrome and testing positive for anti-PLA2R antibodies, the expected finding on renal biopsy is a diffuse thickening of the GBM with a spike and dome pattern, indicative of primary membranous nephropathy.

questions.stem: A 3-week-old neonate presents with increasing jaundice, hepatomegaly, and pale stools. A liver biopsy reveals marked proliferation of bile ducts, portal tract edema and fibrosis, and extensive intrahepatic and canalicular bile stasis. The infant's jaundice worsens progressively, and the infant dies of liver failure at 9 months of age. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Biliary atresia

 

  • Biliary atresia is a condition in which the bile ducts inside or outside the liver are abnormally narrow, blocked, or absent.
  • This leads to bile buildup in the liver, causing progressive liver damage.
  • The clinical presentation includes jaundice, hepatomegaly, and acholic (pale) stools.
  • The liver biopsy findings of bile duct proliferation, portal tract edema, fibrosis, and intrahepatic bile stasis are characteristic of biliary atresia.
  • If untreated, biliary atresia leads to worsening jaundice and liver failure.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Congenital toxoplasmosis: Presents with a range of symptoms including neurological deficits and chorioretinitis, but does not match the liver pathology described here.

 

Option B. α1-Antitrypsin deficiency: Can cause neonatal hepatitis and cholestasis but typically does not present with the severe bile duct proliferation and fibrosis seen in biliary atresia.

 

Option D. Choledochal cyst: Causes cystic dilatation of the bile ducts but is less likely to cause the described severe liver pathology and progression to liver failure seen in biliary atresia.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Biliary atresia is characterized by progressive jaundice, hepatomegaly, and acholic stools in neonates, with liver biopsy showing bile duct proliferation, fibrosis, and bile stasis, leading to liver failure if untreated.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old man presents with increasing enlargement and heaviness in his scrotum for the past year. Physical examination reveals the right testis is twice its normal size, firm, and slightly tender. Ultrasound shows a 3.5-cm solid mass in the right testis. Abdominal CT scan reveals para-aortic lymph node enlargement, and a chest radiograph shows multiple lung nodules. Laboratory findings indicate markedly increased serum levels of chorionic gonadotropin and α-fetoprotein. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.label: C
options.text: Metastatic adenocarcinoma of the prostate gland

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Mixed germ cell tumor

 

  • Mixed germ cell tumors can produce both chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) and α-fetoprotein (AFP).
  • The presence of both elevated serum markers, along with the clinical and radiologic findings, is characteristic of a mixed germ cell tumor.
  • These tumors often contain a combination of different germ cell components, such as teratoma, embryonal carcinoma, yolk sac tumor, and choriocarcinoma.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Leydig cell tumor: These tumors are typically hormonally active but do not produce hCG or AFP.

 

Option B. Pure spermatocytic seminoma: This type of tumor generally does not produce hCG or AFP and is less likely to metastasize.

 

Option C. Metastatic adenocarcinoma of the prostate gland: Would not typically produce hCG or AFP and is less likely to present as a testicular mass with the described findings.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Mixed germ cell tumors often present with elevated levels of both chorionic gonadotropin and α-fetoprotein and are characterized by their combination of different germ cell components, leading to complex clinical and radiologic findings.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman with a 8-year history of progressive dementia dies of bronchopneumonia. Autopsy shows cerebral atrophy mainly in the frontal and parietal lobes. Microscopic examination reveals numerous neuritic plaques in the hippocampus, amygdala, and neocortex. Congo red staining shows amyloid in the cerebral arteries. Which genetic factor is most likely involved in her disease?

options.label: A
options.text: Expansion of CAG repeats on chromosome 4p16

options.label: B
options.text: Inheritance of a mutant prion gene

options.label: D
options.text: Inheritance of the ε4 allele at the ApoE gene

questions.answerText: Inheritance of the ε4 allele at the ApoE gene
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Inheritance of the ε4 allele at the ApoE gene

 

  • The findings of neuritic plaques and amyloid deposition are characteristic of Alzheimer's disease.
  • The inheritance of the ε4 allele of the ApoE gene is a well-known genetic risk factor for late-onset Alzheimer's disease, influencing the formation and deposition of amyloid plaques.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Expansion of CAG repeats on chromosome 4p16: This is associated with Huntington's disease, not Alzheimer's disease.

 

Option B. Inheritance of a mutant prion gene: Associated with prion diseases like Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, not Alzheimer's disease.

 

Option C. HLA-DR3/DR4: Associated with autoimmune diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis and type 1 diabetes, not Alzheimer's disease.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Inheritance of the ε4 allele at the ApoE gene is a significant risk factor for developing late-onset Alzheimer's disease, which is characterized by amyloid plaque formation and cerebral atrophy.

questions.stemHtml: A 38-year-old woman presents with severe fatigue, nausea, and easy bruising for 4 months. Physical examination reveals pustules on her face, splenomegaly, and hepatomegaly. Laboratory tests show hemoglobin of 5.9 g/dL, platelets of 60,000/mL, and a peripheral blood smear is given below. She develops diffuse purpura, gum bleeding, and lab results indicate disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Acute promyelocytic leukemia

 

  • Acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) is a subtype of acute myeloid leukemia characterized by the presence of promyelocytes in the peripheral blood and bone marrow.
  • A hallmark feature of APL is the presence of Auer rods in the malignant cells, as seen in the peripheral smear.
  • Patients with APL often present with symptoms related to pancytopenia (anemia, thrombocytopenia) and a high risk of disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), as described in the case scenario.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Acute megakaryocytic leukemia: This rare leukemia involves megakaryoblasts and does not typically present with Auer rods or DIC.

 

Option B. Chronic myelogenous leukemia: CML is marked by the Philadelphia chromosome and elevated white blood cell counts. It does not feature Auer rods or a high risk of DIC.

 

Option D. Acute lymphoblastic leukemia: ALL commonly affects children and involves lymphoblasts. It lacks Auer rods and the presentation of DIC.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Acute promyelocytic leukemia is identified by promyelocytes with Auer rods and is associated with a high risk of DIC, leading to severe bleeding and pancytopenia symptoms.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy presents with complaints of recurrent bleeding. He has a retroperitoneal hematoma and develops joint pain with swelling upon slight exercise. There is no mucosal bleeding. Which of the following coagulation factors can be responsible for the patient's condition?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Factor 8/9 deficiency

 

  • The symptoms described in the scenario, including recurrent bleeding, retroperitoneal hematoma, and joint pain with swelling (hemarthrosis), are characteristic of hemophilia.
  • Hemophilia is caused by a deficiency in either factor VIII (hemophilia A) or factor IX (hemophilia B).
  • Both conditions lead to similar clinical presentations, primarily involving bleeding into joints and soft tissues without mucosal bleeding.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Von Willebrand factor deficiency: Von Willebrand disease typically presents with mucosal bleeding, such as nosebleeds, gum bleeding, and heavy menstrual periods in females. It does not commonly cause joint bleeding or retroperitoneal hematomas.

 

Option C. Lupus anticoagulant: Lupus anticoagulant is associated with antiphospholipid syndrome, which can cause thrombotic events rather than bleeding disorders. It is not linked to hemarthrosis or retroperitoneal hematomas.

 

Option D. Factor 9/12 deficiency: Factor XII deficiency is generally not associated with a bleeding disorder but rather with a prolonged aPTT without clinical bleeding symptoms. Factor IX deficiency is already covered under hemophilia B, making this option partially correct but misleading due to the inclusion of factor XII.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Hemophilia, caused by a deficiency in factor VIII or IX, leads to recurrent bleeding episodes, retroperitoneal hematomas, and joint bleeding (hemarthrosis) without mucosal bleeding.

questions.stemHtml: A 6-year-old male child presents to the emergency department with a 2-week history of fever and fatigue. He has now developed signs of left ventricular dysfunction, including dyspnea and reduced exercise tolerance. A cardiac biopsy is performed, and the histological image is provided. Which of the following is the likely diagnosis in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Lymphocytic myocarditis

 

  • The histological image shows myocardial tissue with an infiltrate predominantly composed of lymphocytes, which is characteristic of lymphocytic myocarditis.
  • This type of myocarditis is commonly caused by viral infections such as Coxsackievirus and can present with symptoms like fever, fatigue, and signs of heart failure, including left ventricular dysfunction.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Pyogenic myocarditis: Pyogenic myocarditis, caused by bacterial infections, would show a predominance of neutrophils rather than lymphocytes in the myocardial infiltrate. The image does not show neutrophilic infiltration, which rules out this diagnosis.

 

Option C. Chagas disease: Chagas disease, caused by the protozoan Trypanosoma cruzi, typically presents with amastigotes in myocardial cells. The biopsy image does not show these characteristic features of Chagas disease.

 

Option D. Acute rheumatic fever: Acute rheumatic fever usually presents with Aschoff bodies in the myocardium, which are granulomatous nodules, and is part of a pancarditis involving all layers of the heart. The image does not show these specific features.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Lymphocytic myocarditis is characterized by the presence of lymphocytic infiltrates in the myocardial tissue and can present with symptoms such as fever, fatigue, and signs of left ventricular dysfunction, as seen in the provided histological image.

questions.stemHtml: A 42-year old patient underwent cystoscopy, which revealed multiple yellow-white plaques in the trigone of the bladder. The histopathology image is provided. What is the diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Malakoplakia

 

  • Malakoplakia is characterized by the presence of yellow-white plaques in the bladder mucosa, often in the trigone area.
  • Histologically, it features large histiocytes (von Hansemann cells) with basophilic inclusions called Michaelis-Gutmann bodies, which are pathognomonic for this condition.
  • These inclusions are due to defective phagocytosis of bacteria, typically Escherichia coli, leading to a chronic granulomatous inflammatory response.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A.  Interstitial cystitis: Interstitial cystitis, also known as painful bladder syndrome, typically presents with chronic pelvic pain, urinary urgency, and frequency. Cystoscopic findings may include glomerulations (pinpoint hemorrhages) but not yellow-white plaques. Histologically, it shows inflammatory infiltrates, mast cells, and fibrosis.

 

Option C. Polypoid cystitis: Polypoid cystitis is a reactive inflammatory condition of the bladder often associated with chronic irritation, such as from indwelling catheters. It is characterized by the presence of polypoid projections of the mucosa but does not present with yellow-white plaques or the histological features seen in malakoplakia.

 

Option D. Acute cystitis: Acute cystitis presents with symptoms of urinary tract infection, such as dysuria, frequency, and urgency. Cystoscopic findings typically show erythematous and edematous mucosa with petechial hemorrhages. Histologically, it is characterized by neutrophilic infiltration but lacks the hallmark features of malakoplakia.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Malakoplakia is identified by the presence of yellow-white plaques in the bladder and histologically by the presence of von Hansemann cells and Michaelis-Gutmann bodies, indicative of a chronic granulomatous inflammatory response to bacterial infection.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old patient with a history of nephrotic syndrome presents with symptoms of unexplained swelling and recent episodes of leg pain. Laboratory tests show hypoalbuminemia and proteinuria. The physician suspects a hypercoagulable state. What is the cause of hypercoagulation in this nephrotic syndrome?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Loss of antithrombin III (AT III)

 

  • In nephrotic syndrome, there is significant proteinuria, leading to the loss of several important proteins in the urine.
  • One of these proteins is antithrombin III (AT III), a crucial inhibitor of thrombin and other clotting factors.
  • The loss of AT III results in a hypercoagulable state, increasing the risk of thrombosis in these patients.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Decreased metabolism of vitamin K: Decreased metabolism of vitamin K is not a feature of nephrotic syndrome. Vitamin K is essential for the synthesis of several clotting factors, but its metabolism is not directly affected in nephrotic syndrome.

 

Option B. Increase in Protein C: Protein C is a natural anticoagulant. An increase in Protein C would lead to a reduced risk of thrombosis, which is the opposite of what occurs in nephrotic syndrome.

 

Option D. Decreased fibrinogen: Fibrinogen levels are typically normal or increased in nephrotic syndrome. Decreased fibrinogen would lead to a bleeding tendency rather than a hypercoagulable state.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • In nephrotic syndrome, the hypercoagulable state is primarily caused by the loss of antithrombin III (AT III) in the urine, which impairs the body's ability to inhibit thrombin and other clotting factors, thereby increasing the risk of thrombosis.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old male presents with hematuria and flank pain. Imaging studies reveal a renal mass. A biopsy is performed, and histopathological examination shows a characteristic hobnail pattern. In which type of renal carcinoma is the hobnail pattern seen?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Collecting duct carcinoma

 

  • Collecting duct carcinoma, also known as Bellini duct carcinoma, is a rare and aggressive type of renal cell carcinoma.
  • It is characterized histologically by a hobnail pattern, where the tumor cells have a distinct hobnail appearance, often with prominent nucleoli and an infiltrative growth pattern.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Clear cell carcinoma: Clear cell carcinoma is the most common type of renal cell carcinoma and typically presents with clear cytoplasm due to the high content of lipids and glycogen. It does not exhibit a hobnail pattern.

 

Option B. Papillary carcinoma: Papillary renal cell carcinoma is characterized by the formation of papillary structures with fibrovascular cores. It can be further subdivided into Type 1 and Type 2 based on histological features but does not show a hobnail pattern.

 

Option C. Chromophobe cell cancer: Chromophobe renal cell carcinoma is characterized by pale, eosinophilic cytoplasm and prominent cell borders, often described as having a "plant cell-like" appearance. It is not associated with a hobnail pattern.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • The hobnail pattern is a histological characteristic seen in collecting duct carcinoma, a rare and aggressive type of renal cell carcinoma.

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following tests should be performed using the vacutainer shown in the image below?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) TSH levels

 

  • The yellow-top vacutainer contains a serum separator tube (SST) with a clot activator and gel for serum separation.
  • This type of vacutainer is suitable for tests that require serum, such as TSH levels and other biochemical assays.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Complete blood count: A complete blood count (CBC) requires whole blood and is typically performed using a lavender-top vacutainer containing EDTA as an anticoagulant. The yellow-top vacutainer is not suitable for CBCs.

 

Option B. ESR by Wintrobe's method: The erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) by Wintrobe's method requires whole blood with an anticoagulant, typically collected in a black-top or lavender-top vacutainer with EDTA. The yellow-top vacutainer is not appropriate for this test.

 

Option D. Peripheral smear: A peripheral smear also requires whole blood, typically collected in a lavender-top vacutainer with EDTA. The yellow-top vacutainer is not suitable for preparing a peripheral smear.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • The yellow-top vacutainer is used for serum separation and is suitable for tests that require serum, such as TSH levels.
  • It is not appropriate for tests requiring whole blood or plasma, such as a CBC, ESR, or peripheral smear.

questions.stemHtml: A 40-year-old woman presents with a painless, progressively enlarging thyroid mass. She has no significant symptoms of hyperthyroidism or hypothyroidism. A fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the thyroid gland is performed, and the histological findings are shown in the image below. Which of the following best describes the pathologic findings?

options.label: C
options.text: Dense lymphoid infiltrate with germinal centers

options.label: D
options.text: Follicular hyperplasia with scalloping of colloid

questions.answerText: Follicular hyperplasia with scalloping of colloid
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Follicular hyperplasia with scalloping of colloid

 

  • The histological image shows follicular hyperplasia with scalloping of the colloid, which is characteristic of Graves' disease.
  • Graves' disease is an autoimmune disorder that leads to hyperthyroidism and is characterized histologically by hyperplastic thyroid follicles with clear vacuoles (scalloping) at the edges of the colloid, indicating active reabsorption of the colloid.

 

 

 

Other Options

 

Option A. Papillary hyperplasia with psammoma bodies: Papillary thyroid carcinoma is characterized by the presence of papillary structures, often with psammoma bodies (concentrically layered calcifications). The image does not show these features.

 

Option B. Atrophy and fibrosis: Reidel's thyroiditis is characterized by extensive fibrosis and atrophy of the thyroid gland, making it hard and woody in consistency. This is not shown in the image.

 

Option C. Dense lymphoid infiltrate with germinal centers: Hashimoto's thyroiditis is characterized by a dense lymphoid infiltrate with germinal centers, indicating chronic inflammation. The image does not show these features.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Follicular hyperplasia with scalloping of the colloid is characteristic of Graves' disease, indicating an active reabsorption of colloid and an autoimmune cause of hyperthyroidism.

questions.stemHtml: A 57-year-old woman presents with a rapidly growing breast mass. Imaging and biopsy confirm the presence of invasive breast carcinoma. The tumor is evaluated for HER2/neu status using immunohistochemical staining, which shows strong, uniform membrane staining in more than 10% of the tumor cells, as illustrated in the provided image. Which genetic mechanism best explains the observed HER2/neu staining pattern?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Gene amplification

 

  • The strong and uniform staining for HER2/neu indicates overexpression of the HER2 protein, typically due to gene amplification.
  • In breast cancer, HER2/neu gene amplification leads to an increased number of copies of the HER2 gene, resulting in overproduction of the HER2 protein on the cell surface.
  • This mechanism is associated with more aggressive tumor behavior and can be targeted with specific therapies such as trastuzumab.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Polyploidy: Polyploidy refers to cells containing more than two complete sets of chromosomes. While it can be a feature of cancer cells, it does not specifically account for the overexpression of HER2/neu protein.

 

Option B. Chromosomal nonhomologous crossing over: Chromosomal nonhomologous crossing over involves the exchange of genetic material between nonhomologous chromosomes and is not related to the specific overexpression of HER2/neu.

 

Option D. Aneuploidy: Aneuploidy refers to an abnormal number of chromosomes. While aneuploidy is common in cancer cells, it does not specifically result in HER2/neu overexpression.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • The overexpression of HER2/neu in breast cancer is most commonly due to gene amplification, which leads to increased HER2 protein on the cell surface and can be detected by strong, uniform staining in immunohistochemical analysis.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old boy presents with headaches, vomiting, and difficulty with coordination. Imaging studies reveal a mass in the cerebellum. A biopsy of the mass is performed, and histopathological examination confirms the diagnosis of desmoplastic medulloblastoma. Desmoplastic medulloblastoma is associated with which of the following syndrome:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Gorlin syndrome

 

  • Desmoplastic medulloblastoma is a variant of medulloblastoma that is associated with Gorlin syndrome (nevoid basal cell carcinoma syndrome).
  • Gorlin syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by multiple basal cell carcinomas, jaw cysts, skeletal abnormalities, and an increased risk of developing medulloblastomas, particularly the desmoplastic variant.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Cowden disease: Cowden disease, also known as PTEN hamartoma tumor syndrome, is characterized by multiple hamartomas and an increased risk of breast, thyroid, and endometrial cancers. It is not associated with desmoplastic medulloblastoma.

 

Option B. Gardner syndrome: Gardner syndrome is a variant of familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) characterized by multiple colorectal polyps, osteomas, epidermoid cysts, and soft tissue tumors. It is not associated with medulloblastoma.

 

Option D. Turcot syndrome: Turcot syndrome is characterized by the association of colorectal polyposis (as seen in FAP or Lynch syndrome) with primary brain tumors, particularly glioblastomas and medulloblastomas. While medulloblastomas can occur in Turcot syndrome, the desmoplastic variant is specifically associated with Gorlin syndrome.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Desmoplastic medulloblastoma is associated with Gorlin syndrome (nevoid basal cell carcinoma syndrome), which is characterized by multiple basal cell carcinomas, jaw cysts, and skeletal abnormalities.

questions.stem: During an autopsy, an organ is sectioned, revealing a focal, wedge-shaped firm area accompanied by extensive hemorrhage, giving it a red appearance. The lesion has a base on the surface of the organ. This finding is typically indicative of which condition?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Lung with pulmonary thromboembolism

 

  • The description of a focal, wedge-shaped firm area with extensive hemorrhage and a red appearance is characteristic of a hemorrhagic infarct.
  • This type of infarct is typically seen in the lung due to pulmonary thromboembolism.
  • In the lung, the dual blood supply (from the pulmonary and bronchial arteries) can lead to hemorrhage into the infarcted area, resulting in the described appearance.
  • The wedge shape indicates the vascular distribution area affected by the embolus.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Heart with coronary thrombosis: Coronary thrombosis in the heart leads to myocardial infarction, which typically presents as a pale or white area of coagulative necrosis rather than a hemorrhagic infarct.

 

Option C. Liver with hypovolemic shock: Hypovolemic shock in the liver generally causes centrilobular necrosis due to reduced perfusion, not a focal, wedge-shaped hemorrhagic area.

 

Option D. Kidney with septic embolus: Septic emboli in the kidney can cause infarction, but these infarcts are typically pale or white due to the lack of collateral circulation and are not usually characterized by extensive hemorrhage.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • A focal, wedge-shaped firm area with extensive hemorrhage and a red appearance, particularly with a base on the surface of the organ, is characteristic of a hemorrhagic infarct, typically seen in the lung due to pulmonary thromboembolism.

questions.stemHtml: A 53-year-old man presents with worsening dyspnea and cough. Despite treatment, he succumbs to respiratory failure. An autopsy is performed, revealing the lung pathology shown in the image. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis based on the autopsy findings?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Panacinar emphysema

 

  • Panacinar emphysema is characterized by uniform destruction and enlargement of the acini, affecting the entire alveolus distal to the terminal bronchiole.
  • This type of emphysema typically results in large, confluent airspaces, as seen in the autopsy image.
  • Panacinar emphysema is commonly associated with alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, which predisposes patients to extensive lung damage and respiratory failure.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Chronic bronchitis: Chronic bronchitis is marked by chronic inflammation, mucous gland hyperplasia, and excessive mucus production, leading to airway obstruction. It does not produce the large airspaces seen in panacinar emphysema.

 

Option B. Bronchiectasis: Bronchiectasis involves permanent dilation of bronchi and bronchioles due to chronic infection and inflammation, presenting with dilated airways filled with mucus and pus. It does not result in the uniform airspace enlargement seen in panacinar emphysema.

 

Option D. Centriacinar emphysema: Centriacinar emphysema predominantly affects the central parts of the acini, sparing the distal alveoli, and is typically seen in smokers. It primarily affects the upper lobes and presents with a different pattern of lung damage than panacinar emphysema.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Panacinar emphysema, associated with alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, is characterized by uniform destruction and enlargement of the acini throughout the entire alveolus, resulting in large, confluent airspaces and leading to severe respiratory impairment.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department with a history of recurrent bacterial infections. Physical examination reveals growth retardation and distinctive facial features. Laboratory tests show the presence of anti-A, anti-B, and anti-H antibodies. Which of the following disorders is most likely associated with these findings?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) LAD II

 

  • Leukocyte adhesion deficiency (LAD) II is characterized by a defect in the fucosylation process required for the synthesis of the H antigen on red blood cells.
  • This defect leads to the presence of anti-H antibodies, along with anti-A and anti-B antibodies.
  • Clinically, patients present with recurrent bacterial infections, growth retardation, and distinctive facial features due to the impaired immune response and defective leukocyte adhesion and migration.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Bruton's hypogammaglobulinemia: Also known as X-linked agammaglobulinemia, this condition is characterized by a lack of B cells and immunoglobulins, leading to recurrent bacterial infections. However, it is not associated with anti-H antibodies or blood group antibodies.

 

Option B. LAD I: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency I is due to a defect in the integrin β2 chain (CD18), leading to impaired leukocyte adhesion and migration. It presents with recurrent bacterial infections but does not involve anti-H antibodies.

 

Option C. LAD III: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency III involves a defect in the signaling pathway for integrin activation. It presents with recurrent infections and bleeding tendencies, but it is not associated with anti-H antibodies.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • LAD II is characterized by recurrent bacterial infections, growth retardation, and distinctive facial features due to a defect in fucosylation leading to the presence of anti-H antibodies and impaired leukocyte adhesion and migration.

questions.stemHtml: A 52-year-old man presents with chest pain radiating to his left arm and shortness of breath for the past 6 hours. He has a history of hypertension and hyperlipidemia. Physical examination reveals diaphoresis, hypotension, and an S4 heart sound. An ECG shows ST-segment elevations in the anterior leads, and serum troponins are elevated. He is treated with thrombolytic therapy. A biopsy of the heart tissue taken later as shown in the image below. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism responsible for the observed pathology in the image?
questions.solutionHtml: Ans. C) Reperfusion injury

The patient denies any significant trauma or infection at the site, though she did have a cesarean section 2 years ago. On physical examination, a firm, immobile mass measuring approximately 10 cm in diameter is palpated on the lower right abdominal quadrant. A biopsy of the mass reveals bland spindle cells with a collagenous stroma. Which of the following is the underlying pathology in this patient's condition?

options.label: A
options.text: Exuberant proliferation of fibroblasts and collagen

questions.answerText: Exuberant proliferation of fibroblasts and collagen
questions.solutionHtml: Ans. A) Exuberant proliferation of fibroblasts and collagen

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman with a history of multiple transfusions due to recurrent anemia presents to the emergency department with fever and chills 3 hours after receiving a blood transfusion. She denies shortness of breath, chest pain, or dark-colored urine. Her vitals show a temperature of 38.5°C (101.3°F). Physical examination is unremarkable, and the transfusion was stopped promptly. Laboratory workup reveals no evidence of hemolysis. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient’s symptoms?
questions.solutionHtml: Ans. C) Febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reaction

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a severe headache described as "the worst headache of his life." He also reports neck stiffness and nausea. A CT scan of the head reveals subarachnoid hemorrhage. After stabilization, further imaging shows an aneurysm at the bifurcation of the anterior communicating artery. What is the most likely structural defect leading to this type of aneurysm?

options.label: A
options.text: Endothelial injury of the vessel due to hypertension

questions.solutionHtml: Ans. C) Arterial internal elastic lamina defect

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with a history of HIV presents with worsening cognitive function, memory loss, and motor deficits. Imaging shows diffuse cerebral atrophy. Postmortem brain examination reveals the presence of multinucleated giant cells in the cerebral parenchyma. The formation of these giant cells is due to the fusion of which of the following cell types?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Microglial cells

 

Clinical Clues:

 

  • HIV-positive patient with:
  • Cognitive decline, memory loss, motor deficits → Consistent with HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder (HAND)
  • Diffuse cerebral atrophy on imaging
  • Postmortem finding: Multinucleated giant cells in the brain parenchyma
  • These are classic features of HIV encephalitis, a form of neuro AIDS.

 

Pathogenesis:

 

  • HIV enters the CNS early after infection via infected monocytes
  • In the brain, HIV infects microglial cells (the resident macrophages of the CNS)
  • These infected microglial cells fuse, forming multinucleated giant cells
  • The presence of these giant cells is a hallmark of HIV encephalitis

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Oligodendroglial cells: Myelinate CNS axons; not involved in giant cell formation

 

Option B. Neurons: Not infected by HIV and do not form multinucleated cells

 

Option C. Astrocytes: Can be infected by HIV but do not fuse to form giant cells

questions.stem: A 36-year-old man undergoes a biopsy of the small intestine due to chronic diarrhea. Microscopic analysis of the intestinal mucosa reveals a prominent population of immune cells in the intraepithelial region. Which cell type is most likely predominant in the intraepithelial region of the intestine?
questions.solutionHtml: Ans. C) T-cells

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with a history of smoking, systemic hypertension, and emphysema presents to the emergency department with facial swelling and congestion of his head, neck, and upper extremities. His vitals are stable, but on examination, there is prominent venous distention in the upper body. He has smoked for the past 20 years. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml: Ans. D) Superior vena cava syndrome

questions.stem: A 42-year-old man undergoes a colectomy, and the pathologist identifies more than 100 polyps in the resected specimen along with a focus of invasive adenocarcinoma. Genetic testing reveals a mutation in a gene that regulates cell adhesion and growth. What is the functional mechanism of the gene mutation responsible for his condition?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Decreased breakdown of β-catenin

 

Clinical Scenario:

 

  • More than 100 colonic polyps + focus of adenocarcinoma strongly suggests Familial Adenomatous Polyposis (FAP)
  • FAP is caused by a mutation in the APC gene (Adenomatous Polyposis Coli)
  • APC is a tumor suppressor gene that regulates β-catenin degradation in the Wnt signaling pathway.
  • Pathogenesis of APC Mutation:
    • Normally, APC forms a complex with other proteins (like GSK-3β and Axin) to promote β-catenin degradation
    • In FAP, mutated APC fails to degrade β-catenin
    • This leads to accumulation of β-catenin in the cytoplasm and its translocation to the nucleus
    • Nuclear β-catenin activates transcription of oncogenic genes (e.g., MYC, cyclin D1), promoting uncontrolled cell proliferation

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Increased breakdown of β-catenin: Opposite of what happens; APC normally promotes breakdown.

 

Option C. Lack of production of β-catenin: Would impair proliferation, not cause cancer.

 

Option D. Increased nuclear translocation of β-catenin: Is a consequence, not the primary mechanism. The mutation leads to decreased breakdown, which in turn causes increased nuclear translocation.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man undergoes rapid weight loss in preparation for an upcoming role in a film. Shortly after, he begins to experience occasional abdominal discomfort. A HIDA scan reveals slow and incomplete gallbladder emptying in response to cholecystokinin stimulation. Based on these findings, which of the following is the patient most likely to develop?
questions.solutionHtml: Ans. A) Biliary sludge

questions.stem: A 42-year-old man presents with a 2-week history of fever, weakness, and bleeding gums. Peripheral blood smear reveals pancytopenia, and a bone marrow biopsy shows 26% blasts with Auer rods and mature myeloid cells. Additionally, neutrophils with pseudo Pelger-Huet anomaly are detected. Which of the following cytochemical stains is most likely to be positive?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Myeloperoxidase

 

Clinical Clues:

 

  • Fever, weakness, bleeding gums → Suggestive of marrow failure
  • Pancytopenia + >20% blasts in bone marrow = Acute leukemia
  • Presence of Auer rods = Myeloid lineage
  • Pseudo-Pelger-Huët anomaly in neutrophils → Suggests dysplastic changes, commonly seen in myeloid disorders
  • Diagnosis: Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML)

questions.stem: A developing embryo undergoes physiological apoptosis during organogenesis. Which of the following mechanisms is responsible for clearing apoptotic cells without causing inflammation?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Efferocytosis

 

  • Apoptosis is a tightly regulated process of programmed cell death that occurs naturally during development (e.g., digit separation, organ sculpting).
  • To prevent inflammation and autoimmunity, apoptotic cells must be cleared efficiently.'
  • Efferocytosis  

 

Definition:

 

Efferocytosis is the phagocytic clearance of apoptotic cells by macrophages or neighboring cells.

 

Mechanism:

 

  • Apoptotic cells expose "eat-me" signals like phosphatidylserine on their surface.
  • Phagocytes recognize and engulf them → silent removal without triggering inflammation.

 

Importance in embryogenesis:

 

  • Ensures clean, inflammation-free removal during organ development.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Exocytosis:

 

  • Process of expelling materials out of a cell.
  • Not involved in removing dead cells.

 

Option B. Pinocytosis:

 

  • Cell drinking – uptake of extracellular fluid and small molecules.
  • Not specific to apoptotic cells.

 

Option D. Entosis

 

  • Involves one live cell engulfing another live cell (seen in cancer).
  • Not a mechanism for clearing apoptotic cells.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Efferocytosis is the specialized, non-inflammatory mechanism used to clear apoptotic cells during embryogenesis and tissue homeostasis.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man presents for evaluation after receiving multiple vaccinations. A laboratory test is performed to assess his immune response, specifically focusing on the presence of memory T cells that are responsible for long-term immunity. Which of the following markers is most likely used to identify memory T cells?
questions.solutionHtml: Ans. C) CD45RO

questions.stemHtml: A 34-year-old woman presents with a rapidly enlarging neck mass, weight gain, and fatigue. On physical examination, there is a diffuse, non-tender goiter. Laboratory tests reveal elevated TSH and low free T4 levels. A fine needle aspiration biopsy is performed, and the histopathology image is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Hashimoto thyroiditis

 

Clinical Clues:

 

  • Middle-aged woman (34 years)
  • Enlarging neck mass, weight gain, fatigue – all suggest hypothyroidism
  • Diffuse, non-tender goiter
  • Elevated TSH and low free T4 – confirms primary hypothyroidism
  • Histopathology Image Features:
    • Dense lymphocytic infiltration
    • Presence of germinal centers
    • Destruction of thyroid follicles
    • Hurthle cell (oncocytic) change – large cells with abundant eosinophilic granular cytoplasm
  • These are hallmarks of Hashimoto thyroiditis.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Subacute thyroiditis (De Quervain's):

 

  • Usually follows a viral illness
  • Presents with painful, tender thyroid
  • Histology shows granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells, not prominent lymphoid aggregates

 

Option C. Graves' disease:

 

  • Causes hyperthyroidism (↓TSH, ↑T4)
  • Histology: hyperplastic follicles with scalloped colloid, not lymphoid infiltrates

 

Option D. Thyroid adenoma:

 

  • Solitary, well-circumscribed nodule
  • Histology: follicular pattern, no significant inflammation or Hurthle cells

questions.stem: A 23-year-old woman Yashi gives birth to her first child. She begins breast feeding the infant. She continues breast feeding for almost 6 months with no difficulties and no complications. Which of the following cellular processes that began in the breast during pregnancy allowed her to nurse the infant for this period of time?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Lobular hyperplasia

 

  • There is an increase in the breast lobules under hormonal influence, primarily progesterone with pregnancy, to provide for lactation.

 

Other options:

 

Option A. Ductal epithelial metaplasia. Metaplasia is the exchange of the normal epithelium for another in response to chronic irritation.

 

Option B. Stromal hypertrophy. The stroma of the breast consists of connective tissue that provides structural support, but does not have cells that produce milk.

 

Option C. Epithelial dysplasia. Dysplasia in epithelia is a pre-malignant change not part of normal physiologic events. This would be a precursor to breast cancer. Pregnancy is a protective factor against breast cancer.

 

Educational objective:

 

  • During pregnancy, hormonal changes, particularly increased levels of estrogen and progesterone, stimulate the growth and development of the mammary glands in preparation for lactation.
  • This lobular hyperplasia plays a crucial role in enabling women to nurse their infants successfully during the postpartum period.

questions.stem: An adult old man gets burn injury to his hands. Over few weeks, the burned skin heals without the need for skin grafting. The most critical factor responsible for the rapid healing in this case is:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Remnant skin appendages

 

  • In cases of partial-thickness burns, where the deeper layers of the skin including the appendages (such as hair follicles and sweat glands) are preserved, these structures can contribute to the regeneration of the epidermis.
  • The stem cells present in these skin appendages are crucial for initiating the repair process and re-epithelialization, leading to healing without the need for skin grafting.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Underlying connective tissues play a supportive role in wound healing by providing a scaffold for new tissue growth, but they do not directly contribute to the regeneration of the epidermal layer.

 

Option C. Minimal edema and erythema reflect an inflammatory response which is normal in the initial stages of healing. While controlling inflammation can prevent further damage and facilitate healing, it is not the critical factor in regenerating the epidermis.

 

Option D. Granulation tissue is important in wound healing as it fills the wound bed with new connective tissue and capillaries. However, for the re-epithelialization of the skin, especially in the case of burns, the presence of remnant skin appendages is critical.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • In the case of partial-thickness burns, remnant skin appendages containing stem cells are the most critical factor for healing, as they provide the necessary cells for re-epithelialization and skin regeneration.

questions.stem: An infant present with mild anemia, jaundice, and splenomegaly. A complete blood count with differential reveals spherocytosis; with elevated reticulocyte count. The parents state that several relatives have also suffered from a similar illness. The infant’s condition is most likely caused by defective:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Ankyrin

 

  • Hereditary spherocytosis is characterized by the presence of spherical red blood cells on the peripheral smear and is often associated with hemolytic anemia, jaundice, and splenomegaly.
  • This condition is typically inherited in an autosomal dominant manner and is caused by a deficiency or dysfunction of various proteins that make up the red blood cell cytoskeleton, including ankyrin and spectrin.
  • Ankyrin plays a critical role in attaching the spectrin-based cytoskeleton to the plasma membrane, and its deficiency leads to the loss of membrane stability and elasticity, resulting in spherocytosis.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Clathrin is a protein involved in the formation of coated vesicles and endocytosis but is not associated with the pathology of hereditary spherocytosis.

 

Option B. Connexon forms gap junctions that allow communication between cells and is not related to hereditary spherocytosis.

 

Option D. Spectrin is another cytoskeletal protein involved in hereditary spherocytosis, and its deficiency can also cause the condition. However, in the context of this question, ankyrin is the correct answer as it is directly asked for in the question stem.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • The most likely cause of hereditary spherocytosis is a defect in the red blood cell cytoskeleton, commonly involving the ankyrin or spectrin proteins.
  • This leads to spherocytosis, characterized by hemolytic anemia, jaundice, and splenomegaly.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old female patient came for routine examination. On examination, a mid-systolic click was found. There is no history of rheumatic heart disease. The histopathological examination is most likely to show which of the following?

options.label: A
options.text: Myxomatous degeneration and prolapsed of the mitral valve

options.label: B
options.text: Fibrinous deposition on the tip of papillary muscle

options.label: D
options.text: Aschoff nodule on the mitral valve

questions.answerText: Myxomatous degeneration and prolapsed of the mitral valve
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Myxomatous degeneration and prolapse of the mitral valve

 

  • A mid-systolic click is typically associated with mitral valve prolapse (MVP), which is often the result of myxomatous degeneration of the mitral valve.
  • This degeneration involves an accumulation of ground substance in the spongiosa layer of the valve, leading to thickening, elongation, and redundancy of the mitral valve leaflets and chordae tendineae.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Fibrinous deposition on the tip of papillary muscle is not typically associated with a mid-systolic click and is more suggestive of infectious endocarditis or rheumatic heart disease.

 

Option C. Rupture of chordae tendinae would lead to severe mitral regurgitation and typically presents with a new systolic murmur rather than a click.

 

Option D. Aschoff nodules on the mitral valve are characteristic of rheumatic fever, not MVP.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • The clinical finding of a mid-systolic click on cardiac examination is highly suggestive of mitral valve prolapse, which is often due to myxomatous degeneration of the mitral valve leaflets and associated structures.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old male smoker Naresh presents with fever and cough productive of greenish-yellow sputum. The patient states that he has had morning cough with excessive mucus production for the past 5 years. Which of the following abnormalities would most likely be found in this patient?

options.label: D
options.text: Enlarged hilar lymph nodes on x-ray

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Increased Reid index

 

  • The patient's symptoms suggest chronic bronchitis, which is defined clinically by a productive cough for at least three consecutive months in two successive years.
  • An increased Reid index (ratio of the thickness of the mucous gland layer to the thickness of the bronchial wall) is a histological finding consistent with chronic bronchitis, commonly found in smokers.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Apical cavitary lesions on x-ray are more indicative of tuberculosis or lung abscesses.

 

Option B. Curschmann spirals in his sputum. Curschmann spirals are seen in the sputum of asthmatic patients, not typically associated with chronic bronchitis.

 

Option D. Enlarged hilar lymph nodes on x-ray are more commonly associated with sarcoidosis, lymphoma, or metastatic lung disease.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Chronic bronchitis in smokers is characterized by increased mucus production and a corresponding increase in the Reid index due to hypertrophy of the mucous glands in the airways.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy presented with generalized edema. Urine examination revealed marked albuminuria. Serum biochemical examinations showed hypoalbuminemia with hyperlipidemia. Kidney biopsy was undertaken. On light microscopic examination, the kidney appeared normal. Electron microscopic examination is most likely to reveal:

options.label: A
options.text: Fusion of foot processes of the glomerular epithelial cells

options.label: C
options.text: Deposition of electron-dense material in the basement membrane

questions.answerText: Fusion of foot processes of the glomerular epithelial cells
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Fusion of foot processes of the glomerular epithelial cells

 

  • The clinical presentation of generalized edema, marked albuminuria, hypoalbuminemia, and hyperlipidemia is suggestive of nephrotic syndrome.
  • The most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children is minimal change disease (MCD).
  • The hallmark of MCD on electron microscopy is the effacement or fusion of the foot processes of the podocytes (glomerular epithelial cells), despite normal appearance on light microscopy.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Rarefaction of the glomerular basement membrane is not a feature of minimal change disease.

 

Option C. Deposition of electron-dense material in the basement membrane is characteristic of diseases like membranous nephropathy, not MCD.

 

Option D. Thin basement membrane. A thin basement membrane is seen in conditions like thin basement membrane disease (benign familial hematuria), not typically associated with nephrotic syndrome.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • The typical electron microscopic finding in minimal change disease, the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children, is the effacement or fusion of the foot processes of the podocytes.


action of the glomerular basement membrane is not a feature of minimal change disease.

questions.stemHtml: Biopsy of a small, rounded rectal polyp demonstrates glands and sawtooth crypts composed of a proliferation of goblet and columnar epithelial cells as shown in the figure. No atypia is seen. This polyp is best classified as which of the following?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Hyperplastic polyp

 

  • The description of the rectal polyp with sawtooth crypts composed of a proliferation of goblet and columnar epithelial cells without atypia is characteristic of a hyperplastic polyp.
  • Hyperplastic polyps are one of the most common types of polyps found in the colon and rectum and are generally considered benign with a very low risk of progression to colorectal cancer.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Peutz-Jeghers polyp: These are hamartomatous polyps associated with the Peutz-Jeghers syndrome and are characterized by a distinctive arborizing pattern of smooth muscle extending into the polyp.

 

Option C. Tubular adenoma: This is a type of adenomatous polyp that can have a risk of progression to cancer. It typically has dysplastic glandular structures, not the sawtooth appearance of hyperplastic polyps.

 

Option D. Tubulovillous adenoma: This polyp has features of both tubular and villous structures and also carries a risk of malignancy. It would show more architectural and cytological atypia than seen in hyperplastic polyps.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Hyperplastic polyps are characterized by sawtooth crypts composed of a proliferation of goblet and columnar epithelial cells without atypia and are typically benign.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is not a feature of liver histology in non-cirrhotic portal fibrosis?

options.label: A
options.text: Fibrosis in and around the portal tracts

options.label: B
options.text: Thrombosis of the medium and small portal vein branches

options.label: C
options.text: Non-specific inflammatory cell infiltrates in the portal tracts

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Bridging fibrosis

 

  • Non-cirrhotic portal fibrosis (NCPF) is characterized by fibrosis that is typically confined to the portal tracts and does not typically progress to bridging fibrosis or cirrhosis.
  • Bridging fibrosis, which refers to fibrous tissue connecting the portal tracts to each other or to the central veins, is more commonly associated with chronic hepatitis and is a feature that suggests progression towards cirrhosis.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Fibrosis in and around the portal tracts: This is a characteristic feature of NCPF, where the fibrosis is localized within the portal areas and does not typically extend beyond them.

 

Option B. Thrombosis of the medium and small portal vein branches: This can occur in NCPF and is related to the obliteration of portal venules and can contribute to the portal hypertension observed in the disease.

 

Option C. Non-specific inflammatory cell infiltrates in the portal tracts: Inflammation can be seen in NCPF but is generally mild and non-specific.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • The key histologic feature of Non-cirrhotic portal fibrosis is fibrosis within the portal tracts, without the bridging fibrosis commonly associated with cirrhosis.

questions.stem: Bilateral ovarian masses are identified on pelvic examination of a 40-year-old woman for which she undergoes total abdominal hysterectomy. Pathologic examination demonstrates papillary carcinoma producing serous fluid. Which of the following tumor markers would be most useful in monitoring for recurrence?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) CA-125

 

  • CA-125 is a tumor marker that is often elevated in women with ovarian cancer, especially in those with epithelial ovarian cancers such as serous carcinoma.
  • It is useful for monitoring treatment response and detecting recurrence in patients with epithelial ovarian cancer.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Alpha-fetoprotein: This tumor marker is more commonly associated with liver cancer (hepatocellular carcinoma) and germ cell tumors of the ovary, not typically with epithelial ovarian cancers like serous carcinoma.

 

Option B. Bombesin: This is not a standard tumor marker for monitoring ovarian cancer. It has been studied in various cancers but is not routinely used in clinical practice for ovarian cancer.

 

Option D. PSA (Prostate-Specific Antigen): PSA is a tumor marker used primarily to screen for and monitor prostate cancer in men. It is not used for ovarian cancer.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • CA-125 is the most useful tumor marker for monitoring treatment response and recurrence in patients with epithelial ovarian cancer, such as serous carcinoma.

questions.stem: Which of the following techniques can be used to detect exact localisation of a genetic locus?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH)

 

  • Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) is a technique that can be used to detect and localize the presence or absence of specific DNA sequences on chromosomes.
  • FISH uses fluorescent probes that bind to only those parts of the chromosome with a high degree of sequence complementarity.
  • It is a powerful technique for identifying chromosomal abnormalities and for mapping genetic material.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Chromosome painting: This technique involves labelling each chromosome with a different fluorescent dye. It is useful for identifying structural abnormalities in chromosomes but does not provide exact localization of a genetic locus.

 

Option C. Comparative genomic hybridization: This technique is used to detect and map changes in DNA copy number variations across the genome. It compares the DNA content of a test sample to a reference sample to identify gains and losses of genomic material but does not provide precise localization of specific loci.

 

Option D. Western blot: This technique is used for the detection and analysis of proteins. It involves separating proteins by gel electrophoresis, transferring them to a membrane, and detecting them using antibodies. It is not used for localizing genetic loci.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • FISH (Fluorescence in situ hybridization) is the preferred technique for detecting the exact localization of specific genetic loci on chromosomes, as it allows for direct visualization of fluorescently labelled DNA probes bound to chromosomal DNA.
