questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman presents to her primary care physician with a palpable lump in her neck and symptoms of weight loss, tremors, and palpitations. Physical examination reveals a firm, non-tender mass in the anterior neck region. Ultrasonography confirms the presence of a thyroid nodule. Genetic testing reveals a mutation in the RET gene. This gene mutation is associated with which malignancy?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Medullary carcinoma thyroid

 

  • The RET gene mutation is closely associated with medullary carcinoma of the thyroid.
  • Medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) is a neuroendocrine tumor originating from the parafollicular C cells of the thyroid gland.
  • RET gene mutations can be both somatic and germline.
  • Germline mutations of the RET proto-oncogene are also linked to multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN2) syndromes, which include MTC as a prominent feature.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Pheochromocytoma: While pheochromocytomas are associated with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN2) syndromes, which involve RET gene mutations, the tumors themselves are not directly caused by RET mutations but rather are a part of the syndrome.

 

Option C. Lymphoma: There is no direct association between RET gene mutations and lymphomas. Lymphomas are cancers of the lymphatic system and have different genetic associations.

 

Option D. Renal cell carcinoma: RET gene mutations are not directly associated with renal cell carcinoma. Renal cell carcinoma, a type of kidney cancer, has different genetic risk factors, including mutations in the VHL gene among others.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Medullary carcinoma of the thyroid is closely associated with mutations in the RET gene, which plays a crucial role in cell growth and development.
  • These mutations can lead to uncontrolled cell growth and the development of medullary thyroid carcinoma.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a finding in lymphoid tissues in individuals with common variable hypogammaglobulinemia?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Normal B cell count

 

  • In individuals with Common Variable Immunodeficiency (CVID), the lymphoid tissues often show a normal B cell count.
  • Despite the normal quantity of B cells, there is an impairment in the differentiation or function of these cells, leading to decreased levels of serum immunoglobulins (hypogammaglobulinemia) and increased susceptibility to infections.
  • The presence of normal B cell numbers with impaired function is a characteristic finding in CVID.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Decreased B cell count: While some forms of immunodeficiency, such as X-linked agammaglobulinemia, are characterized by decreased B cell counts, CVID typically presents with normal B cell counts in lymphoid tissues.

 

Option B. Increased B cell count: An increased B cell count is not characteristic of CVID. Some other conditions may show lymphoid hyperplasia, but in CVID, the issue is more related to B cell function rather than quantity.

 

Option D. Absent B cells: Complete absence of B cells is not typical of CVID and is more indicative of more severe forms of immunodeficiency, such as X-linked agammaglobulinemia.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Common Variable Immunodeficiency (CVID) is an immunodeficiency disorder where individuals typically have a normal B cell count in lymphoid tissues, but the B cells have impaired function.
  • This leads to decreased immunoglobulin levels and an increased susceptibility to infections.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old female presents with a history of fever and headache and now develops altered sensorium. CT scan shows basal exudates with meningeal enhancement. The CSF is most likely to show:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Lymphocytic pleocytosis, low sugar, high protein

 

  • The presentation of fever, headache, altered sensorium, along with basal exudates and meningeal enhancement on CT scan, is suggestive of tubercular meningitis.
  • Classic CSF findings in tuberculous meningitis:
    • Lymphocytic pleocytosis (predominantly lymphocytes)
    • ↓ Low glucose (due to consumption by bacteria and inflammatory cells)
    • ↑ High protein (due to increased permeability of the blood-brain barrier)

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Lymphocytic pleocytosis, low sugar, low protein: This CSF profile is more typical of viral (aseptic) meningitis, where the glucose levels might be normal or slightly decreased, and protein levels are usually not as elevated as in bacterial meningitis.

 

Option B. Polymorphonuclear pleocytosis, normal sugar, high protein: Polymorphonuclear pleocytosis is initially seen in bacterial meningitis, but the glucose levels are usually decreased, not normal.

 

Option D. Lymphocytic pleocytosis, normal sugar, high protein: This CSF profile could be seen in some cases of viral meningitis or partially treated bacterial meningitis, but the low sugar is a more distinguishing feature of untreated bacterial meningitis.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • In bacterial meningitis, the CSF analysis often shows lymphocytic pleocytosis, low glucose levels due to bacterial consumption, and high protein levels as a result of the inflammatory response.

  • This helps distinguish bacterial meningitis from other types of meningitis such as viral, where glucose levels might be normal or slightly decreased, and protein levels are usually not as elevated.
  • Always think of Tubercular meningitis when:
    • Subacute onset
    • Altered sensorium
    • Basal meningeal enhancement on imaging
    • CSF: lymphocytes + low glucose + high protein

questions.stem: A 15-year-old girl, who was evaluated for short height was found to have an enlarged pituitary gland. Her T4 was low and TSH was increased. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Primary hypothyroidism

 

  • The presentation of a young individual with short stature, an enlarged pituitary gland, low T4 (thyroxine), and elevated TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) suggests primary hypothyroidism.
  • In primary hypothyroidism, the thyroid gland is underactive or not producing enough thyroid hormones (like T4), leading to an elevation in TSH levels as the pituitary gland tries to stimulate the thyroid to produce more hormones.
  • The enlarged pituitary gland could be due to hyperplasia as it overworks to produce more TSH in an attempt to compensate for the low thyroid hormone levels.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Pituitary adenoma: While a pituitary adenoma could cause enlargement of the pituitary gland, it would not typically result in the hormonal profile described (low T4 with high TSH), unless it is a TSH-secreting adenoma, which is quite rare.

 

Option B. TSH-secreting pituitary tumor: This is a rare type of pituitary adenoma that secretes TSH and would typically lead to high levels of both TSH and thyroid hormones (a condition known as secondary hyperthyroidism), which does not match the described scenario.

 

Option C. Thyroid target receptor insensitivity: This condition, also known as thyroid hormone resistance, would lead to elevated levels of both thyroid hormones and TSH due to a lack of feedback inhibition. This does not match the low T4 level described in the scenario.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Primary hypothyroidism is characterized by low levels of thyroid hormones and elevated TSH levels due to the pituitary gland's attempt to stimulate the underactive thyroid.
  • An enlarged pituitary gland in this context could be a result of hyperplasia from the increased production of TSH.

questions.stem: An 11-year-old girl presents with a tibial mass. Histopathological examination reveals a small round cell tumor. Which of the following molecular findings is most likely to be present?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) 22q translocation

 

  • The description of a small round cell tumor in a child, especially involving a long bone like the tibia, is highly suggestive of Ewing's sarcoma.
  • A characteristic molecular finding in Ewing's sarcoma is a translocation involving chromosome 22, specifically t(11;22)(q24;q12).
  • This translocation leads to the fusion of the EWSR1 gene on chromosome 22 to the FLI1 gene on chromosome 11, creating a fusion protein that plays a role in the pathogenesis of the tumor.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. 11q deletion: This genetic aberration is not typically associated with small round cell tumors of bone. Deletions on chromosome 11q are more commonly seen in neuroblastomas and some hematologic malignancies.

 

Option C. 7p translocation: Translocations involving chromosome 7p are not characteristically found in small round cell tumors of bone. They may occur in other types of cancers but are not indicative of Ewing's sarcoma.

 

Option D. n-myc amplification: Amplification of the n-myc gene is a hallmark of neuroblastoma, another type of cancer that can present as a small round cell tumor, particularly in children. However, it is not commonly associated with tumors of the bone like Ewing's sarcoma.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • The presence of a small round cell tumor in a child's tibia, along with the characteristic translocation involving chromosome 22 (t(11;22)(q24;q12)), suggests a diagnosis of Ewing's sarcoma.
  • This translocation results in a fusion gene that contributes to tumor formation.

questions.stem: A middle-aged female presents with headache. Radiological examination reveals 2 cm mass attached to dura. Which of the following will most likely be observed on histopathology?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Psammoma Bodies with Whirling

 

The clinical presentation of headache, along with a mass attached to the dura on imaging, strongly suggests a meningioma. Meningiomas are slow-growing, usually benign tumors originating from the meningothelial cells of the dura. The hallmark histopathological features of meningiomas include:

 

  1. Psammoma bodies: These are concentric, calcified structures often found within the tumor.
  2. Whorled cell arrangements: Tumor cells form concentric whorls, a characteristic feature of meningiomas.

 

Meningiomas are more common in middle-aged women due to their association with hormonal influences, such as estrogen and progesterone receptors.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Fried Egg Appearance: Seen in oligodendrogliomas, characterized by uniform cells with clear cytoplasm resembling fried eggs. These tumors are commonly associated with frontal lobe calcifications.

 

Option B. Antony A and B Areas: Features of schwannomas. Antony A areas are hypercellular, while Antony B areas are hypocellular. Schwannomas may also show Verocay bodies.

 

Option C. Verrucae Bodies: Another feature of schwannomas, consisting of nuclear-free zones seen in Antony A areas.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Meningiomas are dura-attached tumors that show psammoma bodies and whorled arrangements on histopathology. Recognizing their imaging features and histological findings is critical for diagnosis. They are typically benign and may cause symptoms due to compression of adjacent structures.

questions.stemHtml: Match the following microscopic finding with the type of tumor:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) 1-c, 2-d, 3-a, 4-b 

 

  1. Schiller-Duval bodies → Yolk sac tumor (1-c): Schiller-Duval bodies resemble glomeruloid structures and are a hallmark of yolk sac tumors. These tumors are also associated with AFP and alpha-1 antitrypsin positivity.
  2. Presence of teeth, hair, cartilage, etc. → Teratoma (2-d): Teratomas originate from more than one germ cell layer and may contain various tissues such as teeth, hair, and cartilage. Mature teratomas are also referred to as dermoid cysts.
  3. Signet ring cells → Krukenberg tumor (3-a): Krukenberg tumors are metastatic tumors of the ovaries, most commonly originating from gastric adenocarcinoma. Signet ring cells have mucin-filled cytoplasm, pushing the nucleus to the periphery.
  4. Call-Exner bodies → Granulosa cell tumor (4-b): Granulosa cell tumors are sex cord-stromal tumors characterized by Call-Exner bodies, which are small follicle-like structures seen on histology.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Schiller-Duval bodies: Found in yolk sac tumors, associated with AFP positivity.
  • Teeth, hair, cartilage: Found in teratomas (germ cell tumors).
  • Signet ring cells: Found in Krukenberg tumors, often originating from gastric cancer.
  • Call-Exner bodies: Found in granulosa cell tumors, a type of sex cord-stromal tumor.

 

These histopathological features help in diagnosing specific types of tumors.

questions.stem: A patient is having hyperpigmentation on the skin and higher risk for development of skin cancer as per his physician. It is has been due to a DNA repair gene defect. Which of the following is a likely cause of the problem of this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Xerdoderma pigmentosum 

 

Xeroderma pigmentosum (XP) is a rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by a defect in the nucleotide excision repair (NER) pathway, which is responsible for repairing UV-induced DNA damage. As a result:

 

  1. Hyperpigmentation: Occurs due to repeated UV damage and accumulation of DNA mutations in skin cells.
  2. Increased risk of skin cancer: Patients with XP are at a significantly higher risk for developing basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and melanoma at an early age.

 

Key features include:

 

  • Extreme photosensitivity: Patients often experience severe sunburn after minimal sun exposure.
  • Freckling and pigmentation changes: Seen on sun-exposed areas of the skin.
  • Neurological involvement: Can occur in some patients with XP.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Bloom syndrome: Bloom syndrome is caused by a defect in the BLM gene (a DNA helicase), leading to chromosomal instability. Patients exhibit growth retardation, sun-sensitive skin, and increased cancer risk but not hyperpigmentation or specific skin cancer predisposition related to UV damage.

 

Option B. Lynch syndrome: Lynch syndrome (hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer) is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by a mismatch repair (MMR) gene defect. It predisposes to cancers such as colorectal, endometrial, and ovarian cancers but is not associated with skin hyperpigmentation or sensitivity.

 

Option C. Fanconi anemia: Fanconi anemia involves defects in DNA repair pathways, leading to chromosomal instability. It is associated with aplastic anemia, congenital malformations, and increased risk for hematological cancers but not specifically with skin hyperpigmentation or UV-related cancers.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Xeroderma pigmentosum is caused by a defect in the nucleotide excision repair (NER) pathway, resulting in hypersensitivity to UV radiation and an increased risk of skin cancer.
  • It is an autosomal recessive disorder and is distinct from other DNA repair disorders like Bloom syndrome (chromosomal instability), Fanconi anemia (aplastic anemia), and Lynch syndrome (MMR defect).

questions.stem: Which of the following is not true about thromboelastography?

options.label: A
options.text: R time is the time require for clot formation and is dependent on clotting factors

options.label: B
options.text: Maximum amplitude is dependent on platelet activity

options.label: C
options.text: Alpha angle is dependent on fibrin deposition

options.label: D
options.text: Ly30 indicates 30% lysis and is indicator of fibrinlolytic pathway

questions.answerText: Ly30 indicates 30% lysis and is indicator of fibrinlolytic pathway
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Ly30 indicates 30% lysis and is indicator of fibrinlolytic pathway

 

Thromboelastography (TEG) is a test used to evaluate whole blood coagulation dynamics, including clot formation, stabilization, and breakdown. 

 

False. Ly30 (lysis at 30 minutes) does not indicate 30% lysis. Instead, it indicates the percentage of clot lysis that has occurred at 30 minutes after maximum amplitude. It is a measure of the fibrinolytic activity but does not imply a fixed percentage of lysis.

 

Other options:

 

Option A. R time is the time required for clot formation and is dependent on clotting factors: True. R time measures the latency from test initiation to the beginning of clot formation, primarily reflecting clotting factor activity.

 

Option B. Maximum amplitude is dependent on platelet activity: True. Maximum amplitude (MA) represents the strength of the clot, primarily determined by platelet count and function and fibrinogen contribution.

 

Option C. Alpha angle is dependent on fibrin deposition: True. The alpha angle reflects the rate of clot formation, which depends on fibrinogen levels and polymerization.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Thromboelastography (TEG) provides detailed information about the clotting process:
    • R time: Dependent on clotting factors.
    • Alpha angle: Reflects fibrin deposition and polymerization.
    • Maximum amplitude (MA): Dependent on platelet function and fibrinogen.
    • Ly30: Indicates the percentage of clot lysis at 30 minutes, not 30% lysis.
  • It is essential to interpret TEG parameters accurately to diagnose and manage coagulation abnormalities.

questions.stemHtml: A 40-year-old woman has noted painless enlargement of her neck for the past month. On physical examination she has diffuse, symmetrical thyroid enlargement without tenderness on palpation. Laboratory studies show her serum TSH is elevated but serum thyroxine is lower side of normal limits. Her microscopic examination is shown here. Which of the following laboratory test findings is she most likely to have?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) High anti-thyroid peroxidase antibody titre

 

The patient's diffuse, painless thyroid enlargement, elevated TSH with low-normal thyroxine, and histopathological findings of lymphocytic infiltration with germinal centers are characteristic of Hashimoto’s thyroiditis.

 

  • Hashimoto’s thyroiditis is an autoimmune disorder where autoantibodies (anti-TPO, anti-thyroglobulin) attack the thyroid gland, leading to progressive hypothyroidism.
  • The hallmark laboratory finding in Hashimoto’s thyroiditis is high titers of anti-thyroid peroxidase (anti-TPO) antibodies, which are present in >90% of cases.

 

Over time, the destruction of thyroid follicles results in fibrosis and atrophy, leading to permanent hypothyroidism, requiring lifelong levothyroxine replacement therapy.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Increased serum calcitonin: Elevated calcitonin is seen in medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC), which is associated with C-cell hyperplasia and RET proto-oncogene mutations, not Hashimoto’s thyroiditis.

 

Option C. Increased serum parathormone: Parathyroid hormone (PTH) increases in primary hyperparathyroidism, which is unrelated to Hashimoto’s thyroiditis.

 

Option D. Positive antinuclear antibody test: While autoimmune thyroid disorders can be associated with ANA positivity, it is not a specific diagnostic marker for Hashimoto’s thyroiditis. ANA is more commonly used for diagnosing systemic autoimmune diseases like lupus (SLE).

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Hashimoto’s thyroiditis is an autoimmune disorder characterized by high anti-TPO antibody titers and lymphocytic infiltration with germinal center formation.
  • It leads to hypothyroidism with elevated TSH and low-normal/free T4 levels.
  • Levothyroxine is the treatment of choice.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old female presents with excessive bleeding following a minor injury. She has no personal or family history of bleeding disorders. Laboratory testing reveals a prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) that does not correct after mixing her plasma with normal plasma. What is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Acquired factor VIII inhibitor

 

This patient presents with excessive bleeding and an isolated prolonged aPTT that does NOT correct with a mixing study, strongly suggesting the presence of an acquired factor VIII inhibitor (autoantibody against factor VIII).

 

Key Findings in Acquired Hemophilia:

 

  • Autoantibody against factor VIII disrupts the coagulation cascade.
  • Prolonged aPTT due to defective intrinsic pathway.
  • Mixing study does NOT correct aPTT because the inhibitor is still active.

 

Confirmatory Test:

 

  • Bethesda assay detects the presence of factor VIII inhibitors.

 

Causes of Acquired Factor VIII Inhibitor:

 

  • Idiopathic (most common)
  • Autoimmune diseases (e.g., lupus)
  • Malignancies
  • Pregnancy/postpartum period
  • Certain drugs (penicillin, interferon, fludarabine, etc.)

 

Management:

 

  • First-line treatment: Immunosuppressive therapy (steroids, rituximab, cyclophosphamide) to eliminate the autoantibody.
  • Acute bleeding episodes: Bypass agents such as recombinant factor VIIa (rFVIIa) or activated prothrombin complex concentrate (aPCC).

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Hemophilia A:

 

  • X-linked recessive disorder, typically seen in males.
  • Prolonged aPTT that corrects with a mixing study (no inhibitors).
  • Factor VIII deficiency is congenital, not acquired.

 

Option B. Von Willebrand disease (VWD):

 

  • VWD primarily causes mucosal bleeding (e.g., nosebleeds, menorrhagia), not prolonged aPTT without correction.
  • Mixing study corrects aPTT in VWD.

 

Option C. Factor IX deficiency (Hemophilia B):

 

  • X-linked disorder, typically affects males.
  • Prolonged aPTT corrects with mixing study (no inhibitor present).
  • Similar presentation to hemophilia A but involves factor IX deficiency instead of factor VIII.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Acquired factor VIII inhibitor is characterized by spontaneous development of autoantibodies against factor VIII, leading to excessive bleeding.
  • It presents with a prolonged aPTT that does NOT correct with a mixing study.
  • Confirmed by the Bethesda assay, it is treated with immunosuppression (steroids, rituximab) and bypass agents for bleeding control.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the correct statement about liquid biopsy?

options.label: A
options.text: Liquid biopsy primarily relies on the analysis of tissue samples obtained through surgical procedures.

options.label: B
options.text: It is mainly used for the diagnosis of infectious diseases and not for cancer detection.

options.label: C
options.text: Liquid biopsy involves the analysis of biomarkers, such as circulating tumor cells and cell-free DNA, in bodily fluids like blood or urine.

options.label: D
options.text: Liquid biopsy is only used to determine the exact stage of cancer but not for initial detection.

questions.answerText: Liquid biopsy involves the analysis of biomarkers, such as circulating tumor cells and cell-free DNA, in bodily fluids like blood or urine.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Liquid biopsy involves the analysis of biomarkers, such as circulating tumor cells and cell-free DNA, in bodily fluids like blood or urine.

 

  • Liquid biopsy is a minimally invasive diagnostic technique that analyzes biomarkers such as:
    • Circulating Tumor Cells (CTCs)
    • Cell-Free DNA (cfDNA)
    • Exosomes and microRNAs
  • These biomarkers are present in bodily fluids like blood, urine, or cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and provide critical information about tumor genetics and progression.
  • Liquid biopsy is particularly useful for early cancer detection, monitoring treatment response, and identifying emerging resistance mutations.
  • It offers a non-invasive alternative to traditional tissue biopsy and allows real-time tracking of cancer dynamics.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Liquid biopsy primarily relies on the analysis of tissue samples obtained through surgical procedures: Incorrect. Traditional biopsy relies on tissue samples obtained surgically, while liquid biopsy analyzes blood or other bodily fluids.

 

Option B. It is mainly used for the diagnosis of infectious diseases and not for cancer detection: Incorrect.Liquid biopsy is predominantly used in cancer detection, monitoring, and targeted therapy selection, rather than infectious disease diagnosis.

 

Option D. Liquid biopsy is only used to determine the exact stage of cancer but not for initial detection: Incorrect.Liquid biopsy is useful for early cancer detection, identifying minimal residual disease (MRD), and tracking tumor progression.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Liquid biopsy is a non-invasive technique that detects tumor biomarkers like CTCs and cfDNA in blood or urine.
  • It is useful for early cancer detection, monitoring treatment response, and identifying resistance mutations.
  • Unlike traditional biopsy, it does not require invasive procedures and can be repeated multiple times.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old patient presented to the clinic with a history of malabsorption, diarrhea, and poor appetite. Duodenal biopsy of the patient showed crypt hyperplasia, villi atrophy, and CD8+ cells in lamina propria. This patient is kept under regular follow-up to diagnose which of the following malignancies?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Enteric T cell lymphoma 

 

The patient’s clinical history and biopsy findings are highly suggestive of celiac disease (gluten-sensitive enteropathy).

 

  • Key histological features of celiac disease include:
    • Villous atrophy – Loss of normal intestinal architecture.
    • Crypt hyperplasia – Increased depth of intestinal crypts.
    • Infiltration of CD8+ T cells in the lamina propria.
  • Serologic markers of celiac disease include:
    • Anti-endomysial antibodies
    • Anti-tissue transglutaminase (tTG) antibodies

 

Celiac disease is associated with an increased risk of enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma (EATL), a rare but aggressive malignancy. Patients who continue to consume gluten despite being diagnosed with celiac disease are at a particularly high risk.

 

Thus, regular follow-up is necessary to monitor for EATL development in patients with refractory or long-standing celiac disease.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. MALToma: MALT (Mucosa-Associated Lymphoid Tissue) lymphoma is associated with H. pylori infection and primarily affects the stomach, not the small intestine. It is not linked to celiac disease.

 

Option B. Gastric adenocarcinoma: Gastric adenocarcinoma is associated with H. pylori infection, chronic atrophic gastritis, and certain genetic factors. It is not the primary malignancy of concern in celiac disease patients.

 

Option C. Adenocarcinoma of the colon: Colorectal adenocarcinoma is primarily associated with familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP), Lynch syndrome, and chronic inflammatory conditions like ulcerative colitis. It is not the main malignancy associated with celiac disease.

questions.solutionHtml:

Medulloblastoma: highly malignant, arises in the cerebellum, predominantly in children. It typically presents features of increased ICP. On imaging, it appears as a midline mass in the cerebellum.

 

Histologically, has small, round, blue cells with a high N:C ratio. Homer-Wright rosettes, and disseminates CSF pathways.

questions.stemHtml: A 55-year-old male presented with fatigue, infection and left sided abdominal pain. On his workup, on a bone marrow sample that contained a B cell clonal population having TRAP and annexin A1 positivity. All of the following are true for this patient except:

options.label: A
options.text: Smear shows pancytopenia with cells having a characteristic serrated cytoplasmic border

options.label: B
options.text: Molecular testing shall detect BRAF V600E mutation

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Lymph node involvement is common

 

  • LN involvement is rare. Vemurafenib is used.
  • Rare cases that are BRAF V600E mutation negative will be positive for IGHV4-34
  • Lymphadenopathy is rare in classical HCL.
  • Instead, HCL cells prefer spleen and bone marrow, especially the red pulp of the spleen.
  • If lymph nodes are involved, it's atypical or seen in HCL-variant, not classical HCL.

 

Clinical Scenario Analysis:

 

  • 55-year-old man with:
    • Fatigue, infection, and left-sided abdominal pain
    • Suggestive of cytopenia + splenomegaly
  • Bone marrow: B-cell clonal population with:
    • TRAP positivity (tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase)
    • Annexin A1 positivity
    • These features are highly specific for  Hairy Cell Leukemia (HCL)
    • Hairy Cell Leukemia (HCL) is a rare B-cell chronic lymphoproliferative disorder.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Smear shows pancytopenia with cells having a characteristic serrated cytoplasmic border: True. Classic description.

 

  • The leukemic cells have "hairy" projections (cytoplasmic projections), giving the cells a serrated ("hairy") appearance.
  • Peripheral blood often shows pancytopenia (especially monocytopenia).

 

Option B. Molecular testing shall detect BRAF V600E mutation: True. 

 

  • >90% of HCL patients harbor the BRAF V600E mutation.
  • This is a driver mutation and helps distinguish HCL from other B-cell neoplasms like HCL-variant and splenic marginal zone lymphoma.

 

Option D. Excellent prognosis: True.

 

  • HCL has an excellent response to purine analogs like cladribine or pentostatin
  • Long-term remissions are common, with survival often extending over 10–15 years or more.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not correct about TRALI?

options.label: A
options.text: Seen most frequently with fresh frozen plasma

options.label: B
options.text: Pathogenesis is explained by double hit hypothesis

options.label: C
options.text: Anti HLA antibodies of recipient against donor antigens is causative in nature

options.label: D
options.text: Occurs usually within 6 hours of starting transfusion

questions.answerText: Anti HLA antibodies of recipient against donor antigens is causative in nature
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Anti HLA antibodies of recipient against donor antigens is causative in nature

 

TRALI (Transfusion-Related Acute Lung Injury) is a rare but serious complication of blood transfusion, leading to acute respiratory distress. 

 

  • C. Anti HLA antibodies of recipient against donor antigens is causative in nature
    This is false. In TRALI, it is the anti-HLA or anti-neutrophil antibodies from the donor that react with the recipient's leukocytes, not the other way around. These donor antibodies activate neutrophils in the recipient’s lungs, leading to lung injury. So, this statement is incorrect.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Seen most frequently with fresh frozen plasma: This is true. TRALI is most commonly associated with transfusions of fresh frozen plasma (FFP) and platelets, as these components often contain plasma proteins and antibodies that can cause TRALI.

 

Option B. Pathogenesis is explained by double hit hypothesis: This is true. The pathogenesis of TRALI is described by the double-hit hypothesis, where the first hit is the underlying condition of the patient (such as inflammation), and the second hit involves transfusion of blood products containing anti-leukocyte antibodies or biologically active lipids that trigger an immune response in the lungs.

 

Option D. Occurs usually within 6 hours of starting transfusion: This is true. TRALI typically occurs within 6 hours of the initiation of a blood transfusion, often presenting with acute respiratory distress and hypoxemia.

 

Educational Objective:

 

TRALI is caused by donor antibodies (such as anti-HLA or anti-neutrophil antibodies) reacting with the recipient's leukocytes, leading to acute lung injury. This makes Option C the incorrect statement, as it describes the reverse of the actual mechanism.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old male presents with progressive decline in his cardiac function and reduced work capacity. He expired and on autopsy, the microscopic examination of the cardiac tissue revealed a yellow-brown pigment deposited in the cardiac cells. Which of the following is true about the location of the pigment present in this individual?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Perinuclear, intralysosomal

 

The yellow-brown pigment described in this 70-year-old man’s cardiac tissue is lipofuscin, which accumulates with age or in conditions of "wear and tear" - especially in long-lived, post-mitotic cells like cardiac myocytes.

 

Key facts about lipofuscin:

 

  • Origin: Lipofuscin is derived from lipid peroxidation of subcellular membranes.
  • Location: It is stored in lysosomes, often appearing as perinuclear granules.
  • Nature: It is intracellular, perinuclear, and found within lysosomes (thus intralysosomal).
